objectives: Explain progressive overload, the SAID principle, and Selye's General Adaptation Syndrome as the basis of training adaptation.
Distinguish linear from undulating periodization and relate one-rep max to training-load prescription.
Describe hypertrophy mechanisms, the volume-intensity trade-off, plyometrics, and rate of force development.

slides.title: Adaptation: overload, SAID, and the General Adaptation Syndrome
slides.body:
**Strength and conditioning** is the applied science of making athletes stronger, faster, and more resilient. Its theory rests on a few foundational principles that explain why the body changes in response to training.

The first is **progressive overload**: to keep improving, the training stimulus must be increased over time beyond what the body is currently accustomed to. The idea is traditionally traced to the legend of **Milo of Croton**, the ancient Greek wrestler said to have lifted a growing calf daily until it was a full-grown bull. Modern coaches apply it by gradually increasing load, volume, density, or complexity. Without progressive overload, the body adapts to a fixed stimulus and then plateaus.

The second is the **SAID principle**, an acronym for **Specific Adaptations to Imposed Demands**. The body adapts specifically to the type of stress placed on it: heavy low-repetition lifting builds maximal strength, high-repetition work builds local muscular endurance, and explosive movements build power. Specificity governs exercise selection, velocity, range of motion, and energy-system emphasis, ensuring that training transfers to the target sport.

The third is the biological framework underlying both: the **General Adaptation Syndrome (GAS)**, described by the endocrinologist **Hans Selye** in **1936**. Selye proposed that the body responds to any stressor in three stages:

- The **alarm stage**, an initial shock in which performance temporarily drops and fatigue accumulates.
- The **resistance stage**, in which the body adapts and supercompensates, rising above baseline.
- The **exhaustion stage**, reached if the stressor is excessive or unrelenting, in which adaptation fails and performance declines, the territory of **overtraining**.

Applied to training, GAS underpins the **supercompensation** model: a training bout creates fatigue, recovery restores and then overshoots the prior level, and the next stimulus should arrive at the peak of that overshoot. Apply stress too often and the athlete never recovers; apply it too rarely and the gains dissipate.

These three principles interlock. Progressive overload supplies an ever-increasing stressor, the SAID principle ensures the stressor is the right kind, and Selye's GAS explains the time course over which the body alarms, resists, and supercompensates. Every periodized program is, at root, an attempt to manage this stress-recovery-adaptation cycle deliberately rather than by accident.

slides.title: Periodization and the one-rep max
slides.body:
**Periodization** is the planned variation of training over time to manage fatigue, peak for competition, and avoid the exhaustion stage of Selye's General Adaptation Syndrome. Its modern formulation is credited to the Soviet sport scientist **Leonid Matveyev**, whose 1960s model divided the training year into **macrocycles**, **mesocycles**, and **microcycles**, and to the Romanian-American coach **Tudor Bompa**, who popularized periodization in the West.

Two broad schemes dominate:

- **Linear (traditional) periodization** moves gradually from high volume and low intensity toward low volume and high intensity across a macrocycle. An athlete might begin with a hypertrophy block, progress to a strength block, then a power block, and finally a peaking or competition phase. The volume falls and the intensity rises in a steady, monotonic trend.
- **Undulating (non-linear) periodization** varies volume and intensity frequently, within a week or even from session to session. **Daily undulating periodization (DUP)** might rotate a heavy strength day, a moderate hypertrophy day, and a high-velocity power day within the same week. Undulating models exploit more frequent exposure to each quality and may better suit athletes who must maintain several capacities simultaneously.

Research comparisons, including work synthesized by scientists such as **William Kraemer** and the position stands of the **National Strength and Conditioning Association (NSCA)**, generally find both approaches effective, with undulating models sometimes producing slightly greater strength gains in trained lifters because of the variety of stimulus.

To prescribe load precisely, coaches anchor training to the **one-repetition maximum (1RM)**, the heaviest load that can be lifted once with correct form. Training intensities are then set as a percentage of 1RM: roughly **85 to 100 percent** for maximal strength (1 to 5 repetitions), **67 to 85 percent** for hypertrophy (6 to 12 repetitions), and **below 67 percent** for muscular endurance.

Because testing a true 1RM is fatiguing and risky, coaches often estimate it from a submaximal set using prediction formulas. The widely used **Epley formula** is

$$1RM \approx w \times \left(1 + \frac{r}{30}\right)$$

where $w$ is the weight lifted and $r$ is the number of repetitions completed. The **Brzycki formula** is an alternative. These estimates let a coach update loads as an athlete gets stronger without repeatedly testing to failure, tying the abstract logic of periodization to the concrete numbers on the bar.

slides.title: Hypertrophy, volume versus intensity, plyometrics, and rate of force development
slides.body:
**Hypertrophy**, the growth of muscle cross-sectional area, is driven by several overlapping mechanisms identified in modern research, much of it synthesized by the exercise scientist **Brad Schoenfeld**:

- **Mechanical tension**, generated by lifting challenging loads through a full range of motion, is now considered the primary driver. High tension activates mechanosensitive signalling pathways, notably **mTOR** (the mechanistic target of rapamycin), which upregulates **muscle protein synthesis**.
- **Metabolic stress**, the accumulation of metabolites such as lactate and hydrogen ions during higher-repetition work, contributes a secondary stimulus, sometimes described through cell swelling and hormonal responses.
- **Muscle damage**, microscopic disruption that triggers repair, was once emphasized but is now thought to play a smaller and less essential role; excessive damage can even impair adaptation.

At the cellular level, growth involves the activation of **satellite cells**, which donate nuclei to expanding fibers, supporting the myonuclear domain.

A central programming question is the **volume-versus-intensity trade-off**. **Training volume**, often quantified as sets times repetitions times load, is a primary determinant of hypertrophy, with a dose-response relationship up to a point of diminishing or negative returns. **Training intensity**, the load relative to 1RM, is a primary determinant of maximal strength. Because total recoverable work is limited, coaches must allocate it: a meet-prep powerlifter emphasizes intensity, while a bodybuilder emphasizes volume. The two cannot both be maximized at once, a direct consequence of fatigue management and Selye's exhaustion stage.

**Plyometrics**, popularized in the West from the Soviet **shock method** of **Yuri Verkhoshansky** in the late 1960s, train explosive power by exploiting the **stretch-shortening cycle (SSC)**. In the SSC a muscle-tendon unit is rapidly stretched (eccentric phase) immediately before it shortens (concentric phase); elastic energy stored in the tendon and a reflexive contribution from the **stretch reflex** augment the subsequent push. The depth jump is the archetypal plyometric exercise. Effective plyometrics depend on a short **ground-contact time** to capitalize on stored elastic energy.

A key performance variable that strength training improves is the **rate of force development (RFD)**, the slope of the force-time curve, defined as

$$RFD = \frac{\Delta F}{\Delta t}$$

RFD measures how quickly an athlete can produce force, which matters because most athletic actions, such as a sprint ground contact lasting under $0.2$ seconds, allow too little time to reach maximal force. Heavy strength training, ballistic lifting, and plyometrics all improve RFD by enhancing neural drive, motor-unit recruitment speed, and tendon stiffness, linking the molecular biology of hypertrophy to the on-field expression of explosive power.

question.question: An athlete lifts $100\ \text{kg}$ for $5$ repetitions. Using the Epley formula $1RM \approx w \times (1 + r/30)$, estimate their one-rep max in kilograms. Round to one decimal place.
According to current evidence, which mechanism is considered the primary driver of muscle hypertrophy?
options: Muscle damage, because more soreness always means more growth.
Mechanical tension applied through challenging loads, which activates pathways such as mTOR to increase muscle protein synthesis.
Metabolic stress alone, independent of any tension.
Maximal heart rate elevation during the set.
question.explanation: Mechanical tension is regarded as the principal driver of hypertrophy; it activates mechanosensitive signalling, notably mTOR, raising muscle protein synthesis. Metabolic stress is a meaningful secondary contributor, while muscle damage is now thought to play a smaller role and excessive damage can impair adaptation. Heart rate is irrelevant to hypertrophy signalling.

hints: Think about which stimulus directly activates mTOR signalling.
More soreness does not equal more growth.
slides.workedSolution: Modern syntheses of the hypertrophy literature rank mechanical tension as the primary stimulus because it activates mechanosensitive pathways such as mTOR that elevate muscle protein synthesis. Metabolic stress contributes secondarily, and muscle damage, once emphasized, is now considered minor and potentially counterproductive in excess. Hence the mechanical-tension option is correct.

question.question: During an isometric pull, force rises from $0\ \text{N}$ to $1500\ \text{N}$ in $0.30\ \text{s}$. Using $RFD = \Delta F / \Delta t$, compute the average rate of force development in newtons per second. Give the number only.
question.hint: Divide the change in force by the change in time.

question.question: Diagnose and re-plan an athlete stuck on a strength plateau.
question.prompt: A rugby player on a strictly linear periodization plan has stalled: their strength has not improved in six weeks, they feel persistently fatigued, their sleep is poor, and their performance is drifting downward. Using Selye's General Adaptation Syndrome and the volume-versus-intensity trade-off, explain which stage of GAS this picture suggests and why simply adding more load (more progressive overload) could make things worse. Propose how you would adjust periodization, perhaps introducing a deload week or shifting toward an undulating model, and explain how the SAID principle should still guide which qualities you prioritize for a rugby forward.

question.question: Why is the rate of force development (RFD) often more relevant than maximal strength for sprinting performance?
options: Because sprinters never need to produce large forces.
Because ground-contact times in sprinting are very short (often under 0.2 s), leaving too little time to reach maximal force, so how fast force is produced matters more.
Because RFD is identical to the one-rep max.
Because RFD only matters for endurance events.
question.explanation: RFD is the slope of the force-time curve, capturing how quickly force is generated. In sprinting, ground-contact times are often under 0.2 seconds, far less than the roughly 0.3 or more seconds needed to reach maximal force. The athlete who develops force faster applies more force within the available contact time, so RFD frequently predicts sprint performance better than absolute maximal strength.

hints: How long is a sprint ground contact compared with the time to reach peak force?
RFD is about how fast, not how much, force is produced.
slides.workedSolution: Maximal force takes on the order of 0.3 seconds or more to develop, but a sprint ground contact lasts under 0.2 seconds. Within that brief window the athlete cannot reach maximal force, so the slope of the force-time curve, the rate of force development, determines how much force is actually applied. That is why RFD often predicts sprint performance better than the one-rep max, making the second option correct.
